en: The Sutra in Forty-two Sections,
translated by the Śramaṇas Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna from the Western Regions during the Later Han Dynasty.
Formerly, Emperor Xiaoming of the Han dreamed at night of a divine person whose body was golden in color.
A sun appeared above his neck and flew before the palace; his heart was filled with joy, and he took great delight in it.
The next day, he asked his ministers, "What deity is this?"
The versatile scholar Fu Yi said:
"I have heard that in India there is one who has attained the Way, known as the Buddha; he can ascend lightly and fly, and he must surely be a divine being."

Thereupon, the Emperor was awakened to this truth and immediately dispatched twelve men—including the envoy Zhang Qian, Qin Jing, Commandant of the Feathered Forest (Yulin), and Wang Zun, a disciple of the Imperial Academicians—to the country of the Great Yuezhi to transcribe and retrieve forty-two chapters of the Buddhist scriptures.

From within the fourteenth stone casket, he ascended and established a stupa and temple; thereupon, the Way and the Dharma spread abroad, and Buddhist temples were constructed and maintained everywhere.

Those from distant lands who submitted to his transformative influence and wished to become his subjects are beyond counting; the land within the borders became peaceful and tranquil, and all sentient beings have continued to receive his grace and benefit without end to this day.
The Buddha said:

"One who leaves their kin to go forth into homelessness for the sake of the Way is called a śramaṇa. They constantly practice the two hundred and fifty precepts and cultivate the four true paths of practice; with a resolute mind directed toward purity, they become arhats."
An Arhat is one who can fly, manifest transformations, prolong his lifespan, and shake the heavens and the earth;
next is the Anāgāmin; an Anāgāmin is one whose soul ascends to the nineteenth heaven at the end of life, where he attains Arhatship;
next is the Sakṛdāgāmin; a Sakṛdāgāmin is one who goes up once and returns once, after which he immediately attains Arhatship.
Next is the *srotāpanna*. One who is a *srotāpanna* undergoes seven deaths and seven births before attaining *arhatship*.
As for the severance of craving and desire, it is like the severing of one's four limbs; they can no longer be used.
The Buddha said:

"Shave off your hair and beard, become a śramaṇa, receive the Way and its Dharma, abandon worldly wealth and possessions, and live on what you obtain through alms; eat but one meal at midday and stay but one night under a tree, being careful not to exceed these limits!"
"That which renders people foolish and debased is attachment and desire.
The Buddha said,
"Sentient beings regard ten things as good, and they also regard ten things as evil."
Three of the body, four of speech, and three of the mind.
The three of the body are:
killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;
The four [misdeeds] of speech are:
double-tongued speech, harsh abuse, false speech, and frivolous chatter;
the three [misdeeds] of mind are:
Envy, anger, and delusion; lack of faith in the Triple Gem; and taking what is false for truth—these are the obstacles.
If an upāsaka practices these five matters without slackening or retreating until he reaches the ten matters, he will certainly attain the Way.
The Buddha said:
"If a person has many transgressions yet does not repent, and fails to still the mind, then sins will return to their body like water flowing to the sea, naturally becoming deep and vast.
If one recognizes evil as wrong and reforms to attain goodness, sins will be extinguished day by day, and in the future, one shall attain the Way."
The Buddha said:
"When people treat me with folly and consider me unwholesome, I protect and deliver them with the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness.
When they come toward me with grave evil, I respond with even greater goodness; the vital energy of merit and virtue always resides here."
"The heavy calamity of this harmful influence has, on the contrary, fallen upon him.
Hearing that the Way of the Buddha maintains great benevolence and compassion—responding with goodness to those who come with evil—he came to revile him.
The Buddha remained silent and did not answer, pitying him for being thus rendered by delusion, darkness, madness, and folly.
When the abuse ceased, he asked:
"If you approach another with courtesy and that person does not accept it, how do you truly regard that courtesy?"
He said, "Take it back.
[The other] replied, "Now you have insulted me, and I will not accept it; you must take it back yourself, for it will bring calamity upon your own person!"
"It is like an echo responding to a sound or a shadow following a form; one can never escape them. Be cautious in committing evil.
The Buddha said:
"When an evil person harms a virtuous one, it is like spitting upward toward the sky; the spit does not defile the sky, but returns to defile one's own body."
"When one throws dust against the wind at another person, the dust does not soil them; instead, it returns and soils one's own body.
A worthy person cannot be defamed; the calamity will surely destroy oneself.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"When a person practices the Way, they must strive for broad love; in extending compassion and bestowing virtue, there is no gift greater than this.
To maintain one's resolve and uphold the Way brings immense merit;
likewise, seeing others bestow the Way and rejoicing in their assistance also secures a reward of merit."
The questioner asked,
"Should his merit not diminish?
The Buddha said:

"It is like a torch: if a thousand or ten thousand people each come with their own torches to take fire from it and go away, using it to cook food and dispel the darkness, that original fire remains as it was;
the merit is likewise."

The Buddha said: "Feeding one hundred ordinary people is not as good as feeding one virtuous person; feeding one thousand virtuous persons is not as good as feeding one person who observes the five precepts; feeding ten thousand who observe the five precepts is not as good as feeding one *srotāpanna*; feeding one million *srotāpannas* is not as good as feeding one *sakṛdāgāmin*; feeding ten million *sakṛdāgāmins* is not as good as feeding one *anāgāmin*; feeding one hundred million *anāgāmins* is not as good as feeding one *arhat*; feeding one billion *arhats* is not as good as feeding one *pratyekabuddha*; feeding ten billion *pratyekabuddhas* is not as good as using the teaching of the Three Honored Ones to deliver one's parents for a single lifetime; and teaching one's parents [to do so] for ten trillion lifetimes is not as good as feeding one Buddha—one who studies and aspires to Buddhahood, desiring to rescue all sentient beings."

"To feed a virtuous person brings the deepest and most profound merit. When ordinary people serve Heaven, Earth, and the spirits, it is not equal to being filial toward one's parents; for one's two parents are the supreme deities.
The Buddha said:
"In the world there are five hardships:"

It is difficult for the poor to practice giving; it is difficult for the wealthy and noble to study the Way; it is difficult to master one's life and avoid death; it is difficult to encounter the Buddha’s sutras; and it is difficult to be born in an age when a Buddha dwells in the world.
A śramaṇa asked the Buddha:
"By what causes and conditions does one attain the Way?
How does one know past lives?"
The Buddha said: "The Way has no form; knowing it is of no benefit. One must simply maintain one's will and practice.

It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is removed, the brightness remains, and one naturally sees one's own reflection. By severing desire and maintaining emptiness, one immediately perceives the truth of the Way and knows past lives."
The Buddha said:
"What is wholesome? Only the practice of the Path is wholesome."
What is greatest?
The union of the will with the Way is greatest.
What possesses the most power?
Patience is the supreme strength; the patient person harbors no resentment and will surely be honored by others.
What is most luminous?
When the defilements of the mind are removed and evil deeds are extinguished, one is inwardly pure and without blemish.

From before the existence of heaven and earth until this very day, regarding all that exists throughout the ten directions—even those sprouts not yet seen—one knows nothing that is unknown, sees nothing that is unseen, and hears nothing that is unheard; having attained all-encompassing wisdom, one may truly be called enlightened.
The Buddha said:

"A person who harbors craving and desire does not see the Path. It is like turbid water into which five colors are cast and stirred with effort; though many people gather at the water's edge, none can see their own reflections.
When craving and desire entwine, the mind becomes turbid, and for this reason one does not see the Path."
When water is clear and impurities removed, being pure and stainless, one immediately sees one's own reflection.
When a fierce fire is lit beneath a cauldron and the water within surges and boils, even if one covers it with cloth, sentient beings looking down upon it likewise cannot see their own shadows;
so too, when the three poisons originally present within the mind surge and boil inside, and the five hindrances cover the outside, one ultimately does not see the Way.
Only when the defilements of the mind are exhausted will one know where the soul has come from, the direction toward which birth and death tend, and the locations of the Buddha-lands and the Way.
The Buddha said:

"One who practices the Way is like someone holding a torch and entering a dark room; the darkness immediately vanishes while the light remains. When one studies the Way and perceives the Truth, ignorance is utterly extinguished, and there is nothing that is not seen."
The Buddha said:
"How could I have any thought that is not the Way?
How could I have any practice that is not the Way?"
"What words can I use to speak of the Way?
I contemplate the Truth of the Way without neglecting it for even a moment.
The Buddha said:

"Behold heaven and earth and contemplate their impermanence; behold the mountains and rivers and contemplate their impermanence; behold the flourishing forms and bodies of all things and contemplate their impermanence.
If you maintain such a state of mind, you will swiftly attain the Way."
The Buddha said:
"If one practices for a single day, constantly mindful of the Way and practicing the Way, one will eventually attain the faculty of faith; the merit thereof is immeasurable.
The Buddha said:

"I have reflected deeply upon the four great elements within my body; names exist only as names and are ultimately non-existent. That which we call 'self' is but a temporary lodging; this life is likewise not long-lasting, for its nature is like an illusion."
The Buddha said:
"When a person pursues fame according to their passions and desires, it is like burning incense; while others smell its fragrance, the incense itself is consumed by its own smoke.
The fool covets the reputation of the vulgar world and fails to preserve the truth of the Way. This fame is a calamity that endangers oneself, and the regret will come later."
The Buddha said:

"Wealth and sensual pleasures are to humans like a child’s craving for honey on the edge of a blade; the sweetness is not enough to satisfy a single meal, yet it carries the danger of severing the tongue."
The Buddha said:
"A person's bondage to wife, children, treasures, and dwellings is a calamity more severe than prison, shackles, or heavy chains.

While there may be pardons for those in prison, regarding the passions for one's wife and children, even if they bring the disaster of a tiger's maw, one still willingly casts oneself therein; such a transgression knows no pardon."
The Buddha said:
"In the realm of craving and desire, none is more profound than form; as for the desire for form, its magnitude is without limit.
If one relies upon even a single [form], let alone two, then among the people under heaven, none would be able to practice the Way."
The Buddha said:
"Desire for people is like holding a torch while walking against the wind.
If a fool does not let go of the torch, he will surely suffer the calamity of burning his hand."

The poisons of greed, anger, and delusion reside within the human body; if one does not early on eliminate these calamities through the Way, there will surely be perilous disaster, just as a foolish and greedy person holding a torch burns his own hand.
A celestial deity presented a jade maiden to the Buddha, desiring to test the Buddha’s intentions and observe his Way.
The Buddha said:
"A leather bag filled with various impurities—what have you come here for?"
"Since you conform to worldly customs, it is difficult for you to move with the six supernormal powers.
Begone! I have no use for you."
The deva, surpassing all in his reverence for the Buddha, took the opportunity to inquire about the meaning of the Way;
the Buddha explained it for him, and he immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The Buddha said:
"Now, one who practices the Way is like a log floating upon the water, following the current as it goes, neither touching the left bank nor the right bank;
it is not seized by people, nor obstructed by ghosts or spirits, nor held back by eddies, nor does it rot. I guarantee that it will reach the sea."
If a person practices the Way, without being deluded by sensual desires or deceived by various evils, and proceeds with diligence and without doubt, I guarantee that they shall attain the Way.
The Buddha told the śramaṇa:
"Be careful not to trust your own mind; the mind can never be trusted.
Be careful not to associate with forms; when one associates with forms, calamity arises."
"Only when you have attained the path of Arhatship can your mind be trusted.
The Buddha told the śramaṇas:
"Be careful not to look at women; if you see one, do not look."
Be careful not to speak with them; if you must speak with them, admonish your mind and rectify your conduct, saying:
"I am a śramaṇa dwelling in this turbid world; I shall be like a lotus flower, unsullied by the mud."
"The elderly he shall regard as mothers, the seniors as elder sisters, the juniors as younger sisters, and the children as his own offspring, honoring them with propriety.

He should then, with focused and earnest contemplation, examine himself from head to foot within; seeing what truly exists in that body, he realizes it contains nothing but a collection of foul secretions and various impure substances, thereby resolving his thoughts.
The Buddha said:
"When a person practices the Way, they must eliminate passion and desire, just as one sees fire in the grass and moves away when it approaches.
When a practitioner of the Way encounters sensual desire, they must certainly distance themselves from it."
The Buddha said:
"There was once a man afflicted by lust whose passion would not cease; he sat upon the edge of a hatchet to cut off his own genitals.
The Buddha said to him:"
"If one severs the aggregates as one would sever the mind, it is because the mind is the chief minister; if the chief minister is stopped, his followers will all cease.
If the deviant mind is not stopped, what benefit is there in severing the aggregates?"
“Will he die in this very instant?
The Buddha said,
“The inverted views of worldly people are like those of such a foolish man.”
There was a courtesan who had made a vow with a certain man; when the appointed time arrived and he did not come, she repented, saying:
"I wish to know the origin of you, my desire: it arises from conceptualization. If I do not conceptualize you, then you will cease to arise."
The Buddha heard this while walking on his almsround and said to the śramaṇa,
"Memorize it!
This is a verse from the time of Kāśyapa Buddha that has circulated among the laity."
The Buddha said:
"From craving arises sorrow; from sorrow arises fear.
Where there is no craving, there is no sorrow; where there is no sorrow, there is no fear."
The Buddha said:

"A person practicing the Way is like a single man fighting ten thousand men. He dons armor, takes up weapons, and steps out his gate intending to fight; yet, with a timid mind and weak resolve, he retreats on his own, or returns halfway, or perishes in the struggle, or achieves a great victory and returns to his country to receive high promotion."

If a person can firmly maintain their mind and advance with vigor and acumen, undisturbed by the deluded and foolish words of worldly custom, desiring to extinguish evil entirely, they will surely attain the Way.
There was a śramaṇa who, while reciting the sūtras at night with great pathos, felt regret and doubt in his mind and desired to return home.
The Buddha called the śramaṇa and asked him,
"When you were living at home, what did you practice?"
He replied,
“I constantly play the lute.
The Buddha said:
"What if the strings were too loose?
He replied,
"They would not sound."
[The Master asked,] "What if the strings are too tight?
[The disciple] replied,
"The sound ceases."
"How is it that the swift and the slow attain the middle way?
"All sounds are universally sorrowful.
The Buddha told the śramaṇa:
"In the study of the Way it is likewise: if one maintains a mind that is harmonious and well-adjusted, the Way can be attained.
The Buddha said, "When a person practices the Way, it is like forging iron; as one gradually deepens the work and discards the dross, the vessel that is formed will surely be excellent."
In studying the Way, one proceeds gradually toward depth, removing the defilements of the mind and applying oneself with diligence to the Path.

If one is violent, the body becomes exhausted; when the body is exhausted, the mind becomes troubled; when the mind is troubled, practice regresses; and when practice regresses, one accumulates transgressions.
The Buddha said:
"For humans, practicing the Way is suffering, and not practicing the Way is also suffering.
From birth to old age, from old age to sickness, and from sickness to death, the suffering of human beings is immeasurable."
"With a mind afflicted by accumulated sins, one does not cease from birth and death; its suffering is difficult to describe.
The Buddha said:
"For a person to leave the three evil realms and obtain a human existence is difficult; "
Having already attained human birth, it is difficult to leave the female state and become male;
having already attained masculinity, it is difficult for the six sense faculties to be fully intact;
and once the six sense faculties are complete, it is difficult to be born in a central land.
To dwell in the Middle Kingdom is difficult; to encounter the Buddha’s Way while dwelling there is difficult;
to serve a sovereign who upholds the Way while following the Buddha’s Way is difficult; to be born into a family of Bodhisattvas is difficult;
and having been born into a family of Bodhisattvas, to have a mind that faithfully believes in the Triple Gem and to encounter the age of a Buddha is difficult.
The Buddha asked the śramaṇas:
"In what interval does a person's life reside?
They replied:
"In only a few days," the Buddha said,
"you have not yet been able to practice the Way."
He asked another śramaṇa:
"In how much time does a person's life reside?
He replied:
"During the time of eating," the Buddha said,
"you are not yet able to practice the Way."
He further asked another śramaṇa:
"In how much time does a person's life reside?
He replied:
"Between breaths," the Buddha said,
"Excellent!"
"You may be called one who has realized the Way.
The Buddha said, "A disciple may depart from me by several thousand li; yet if they keep my precepts in mind, they will surely attain the Way."
If one stands to my left with a mind set on what is heterodox, one will ultimately not attain the Way.
In truth, it is through practice that one realizes it; if one remains close yet does not practice, how could there be even a fraction of benefit?
The Buddha said:
"When a person practices the Way, it is like eating honey; it is sweet both in the center and at the edges.
My sutras are likewise: their meanings are all delightful, and those who practice them shall attain the Way."
The Buddha said:
"When a person practices the Way, they are able to uproot the roots of craving and desire; it is like plucking hanging beads—one by one, they will eventually be exhausted."
"When evil is exhausted, one attains the Way.
The Buddha said:

"When śramaṇas practice the Way, they should be like an ox carrying a load through deep mud; though utterly exhausted, it does not dare look left or right, desiring only to leave the mud behind so as to find rest for itself."
“A śramaṇa regards sensual desires as worse than that mud; by maintaining a straightforward mind and contemplating the Way, one may escape all suffering.
The Buddha said:
“I regard the rank of a feudal lord as a passing guest; I regard treasures of gold and jade as pebbles and stones; I regard the beauty of fine cotton and silk as tattered rags.”
The Sutra of Forty-two Sections (Sishier zhang jing)
